Matching Accuracy, Different Geometry: Evolution Strategies vs GRPO in LLM Post-Training

William Hoy Affiliation:  Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, University of Miami Affiliation: wjh58@miami.edu    Binxu Wang ††thanks: Equal advising. Affiliation:  Kempner Institute, Harvard University Affiliation: binxu.wang@hms.harvard.edu    Xu Pan 11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation:  Harvard University Affiliation: xupan@fas.harvard.edu
Abstract

Evolution Strategies (ES) have emerged as a scalable gradient-free alternative to reinforcement learning based LLM fine-tuning, but it remains unclear whether comparable task performance implies comparable solutions in parameter space. We compare ES and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) across four tasks in both single-task and sequential continual-learning settings. ES matches or exceeds GRPO in single-task accuracy and remains competitive sequentially when its iteration budget is controlled. Despite this similarity in task performance, the two methods produce markedly different model updates: ES makes much larger changes and induces broader off-task KL drift, whereas GRPO makes smaller, more localized updates. Strikingly, the ES and GRPO solutions are linearly connected with no loss barrier, even though their update directions are nearly orthogonal. We develop an analytical theory of ES that explains all these phenomena within a unified framework, showing how ES can accumulate large off-task movement on weakly informative directions while still making enough progress on the task to match gradient-based RL in downstream accuracy. These results show that gradient-free and gradient-based fine-tuning can reach similarly accurate yet geometrically distinct solutions, with important consequences for forgetting and knowledge preservation. The source code is publicly available.11 1 https://github.com/Bhoy1/ESvsGRPO

1 Introduction

Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) is essential for adapting them to new tasks and for maintaining performance in continual learning settings. When explicit supervised targets are unavailable, optimization must proceed from evaluative feedback rather than token-level labels. In this regime, gradient-based reinforcement learning methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) have become a standard component of LLM post-training (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025), while Evolution Strategies (ES) have recently emerged as a scalable gradient-free alternative (Qiu et al., 2025; Korotyshova et al., 2025; Sarkar et al., 2025). ES replaces backpropagation with population-level perturbation and reward aggregation, offering potential advantages in memory usage and parallelism.

Despite growing interest in ES for LLM alignment and fine-tuning, its behavior relative to gradient-based methods remains poorly understood. Prior works present a mixed picture. Some studies (Qiu et al., 2025) suggest that ES can achieve competitive performance while retaining low KL divergence to the base model. This raises the possibility that it may be well suited for continual learning, where preserving prior capabilities is important. Other work (Abdi et al., 2026), however, finds that ES can induce substantial forgetting, attributing this to larger and less sparse parameter updates. Taken together, these results leave open a basic question: when ES and gradient-based RL achieve similar task performance, do they induce similar off-target effects (e.g. forgetting), and do the solutions have similar geometric properties (e.g. norm and dimensionality)?

In this study, we compare ES and RL in a setup where an LLM is trained sequentially across four diverse tasks and extend the analysis with a geometric characterization of the solutions each method finds. Our analysis reveals that despite equivalent accuracy across four diverse tasks, ES and GRPO navigate the loss landscape in different ways. GRPO identifies a narrow, high gradient direction, making precise and targeted updates that stay close to the base model. ES navigates a broad, low curvature plateau, accumulating large diffuse updates that travel orders of magnitude further from initialization. Strikingly, despite these near orthogonal trajectories and orders of magnitude norm differences, no loss barrier exists between the two solutions. Moreover, when we probe the loss landscape along each method’s learned update direction, the ES direction behaves much more like a random direction on held-out tasks, indicating that a substantial fraction of its displacement lies in task-irrelevant dimensions rather than in a sharply task-aligned subspace.

Finally, we derive a theoretical account of these differences, showing how ES can accumulate large off-task movement on weakly informative directions while still making enough progress on the task to match gradient-based RL in downstream accuracy. ES weight updates decompose into two components: an on-manifold component where loss changes, and an off-manifold component that is loss-invariant and therefore performs a random walk through parameter space. The off-manifold component carries a characteristic scaling: the squared norm of the weight change grows as α2​d​T/N\alpha^{2}dT/N, proportional to parameter dimension dd and step count TT, and inversely proportional to population size NN. In the high-dimensional loss landscapes with many flat dimensions, where most directions carry negligible curvature — this off-manifold drift dominates the weight change. Empirically, LLM parameters (particularly weight matrices) precisely exhibit this predicted random walk behavior, with the theoretical scaling matching observations at R2>0.99R^{2}>0.99. This single mechanism accounts for all the geometric phenomena we observe: the large update norm, the near-orthogonality between ES and GRPO update directions, the flat loss curvature along ES weight changes, and the linear mode connectivity despite geometric separation.

Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    Empirical evidence that ES can match or exceed GRPO in task accuracy across both single-task and sequential fine-tuning settings.

  2. 2.

    A geometric characterization of ES versus GRPO solutions, revealing that equivalent task performance can be achieved with orders of magnitude norm differences.

  3. 3.

    A theoretical account of the random-walk-like behavior of ES in high-dimensional weakly informative subspaces, explaining its large update norms and diffuse-like behavior relative to GRPO.

2 Related Work

Evolution strategies for LLMs.

Salimans et al. (2017) demonstrated ES as a scalable alternative to reinforcement learning via high parallelizability. Recent work has brought ES to LLM scale: Qiu et al. (2025) showed ES achieving comparable performance to GRPO on reasoning tasks, attributing this to LLMs’ low intrinsic dimensionality (Aghajanyan et al., 2021) and ES’s smoothing of jagged reward landscapes via Gaussian convolution in parameter space (Lehman et al., 2018). Korotyshova et al. (2025) and Sarkar et al. (2025) further showed that ES can be made practical for large-scale alignment through low-rank parameterizations that improve efficiency and scalability. Liang et al. (2026) showed that fine-tuning loss landscapes are low-dimensional in curvature, helping explain why ES succeeds with small populations. However, Abdi et al. (2026) demonstrates that ES causes significant forgetting compared to GRPO on smaller models (Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama-3.2-1B), attributing it to larger update norms and lower sparsity.

Gradient-based RL for LLMs.

Shao et al. (2024) introduced GRPO, which eliminates the critic model by estimating advantages from group statistics, reducing memory overhead compared to PPO. It became a standard post-training method following its use in DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025). Several concurrent works have investigated why GRPO preserves prior capabilities during fine-tuning. Shenfeld et al. (2025) showed that forgetting correlates with KL divergence from the base model, while Chen et al. (2025) showed that GRPO’s robustness may stem more from its use of on-policy data rather than KL regularization or advantage estimation.

3 Methodology

We compare two fundamentally different approaches to fine tune large language models: ES, a gradient free method, and GRPO, a gradient based reinforcement learning algorithm.

3.1 Evolution strategies

ES optimizes model parameters through population based search without computing gradients. At each iteration, we sample NN perturbation vectors ϵi∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), evaluate the perturbed models, and update parameters using z score normalized rewards:

θt+1=θt+α⋅1N∑i=1NZiϵi\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}+\alpha\cdot\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}\epsilon_{i} (1)

where α\alpha is the learning rate, Zi=Ri−μRσRZ_{i}=\frac{R_{i}-\mu_{R}}{\sigma_{R}} is the z score normalized reward for the ii-th perturbation, and Ri=R⁡(θt+σ​ϵi)R_{i}=R(\theta_{t}+\sigma\epsilon_{i}) is the reward of the perturbed model with noise scale σ\sigma. Following Qiu et al. (2025), we maintain α=σ/2\alpha=\sigma/2 throughout and apply ES updates to the complete model weights.

3.2 Group relative policy optimization

GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) normalizes advantages within groups of sampled responses, eliminating the need for a critic model. For a prompt xx, we sample KK responses {y1,…,yK}\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{K}\} from the current policy πθ\pi_{\theta} and compute group-normalized advantages: A^i=R⁡(yi)−μRσR+ϵ\hat{A}_{i}=\frac{R(y_{i})-\mu_{R}}{\sigma_{R}+\epsilon}, where μR\mu_{R} and σR\sigma_{R} are the within group mean and standard deviation of rewards. The policy is updated by maximizing the clipped surrogate objective: ℒGRPO​(θ)=𝔼⁡[1K​∑i=1Kmin⁡(ρi​(θ)​A^i,clip​(ρi​(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)​A^i)]\mathcal{L}_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\min\left(\rho_{i}(\theta)\hat{A}_{i},\text{clip}(\rho_{i}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat{A}_{i}\right)\right], where ρi​(θ)=πθ​(yi|x)πθold​(yi|x)\rho_{i}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}|x)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(y_{i}|x)} is the probability ratio between the current and old policy. We disable the KL penalty (βKL=0\beta_{\text{KL}}=0) during training to induce a clean comparison with ES without explicit regularization (Shenfeld et al., 2025), but track KL divergence to the reference policy for analysis in both methods.

3.3 Experimental setup

All experiments use Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as the base model. We evaluate on four diverse tasks spanning reasoning, mathematics, scientific knowledge, and reading comprehension: Countdown (arithmetic reasoning), Math (mathematical problem solving), SciKnowEval-Chemistry (chemistry domain knowledge), and BoolQ (boolean reading comprehension). Each task uses 200 training samples and 2,000 test samples (500 for Math). In the continual learning experiments, tasks are presented sequentially. Hyperparameter sweeps were conducted for both methods (see Appendix B.1); we selected N=30N=30, σ=0.0015\sigma{=}0.0015, α=0.00075\alpha{=}0.00075 for ES and lr=1×10−5\text{lr}{=}1{\times}10^{-5} for GRPO.

4 Empirical Results

4.1 Task performance

Table 1 compares the task accuracy of the base model against ES and GRPO in a single task training setup. Running ES for 300 iterations consistently yields the highest peak accuracy across all four tasks. For instance, on the Chemistry task, ES (300) achieves 76.5% accuracy, significantly outperforming both ES (100) at 68.1% and GRPO at 74.9%.

However, when the model is trained sequentially across the tasks (Figure 1), utilizing 300 ES iterations causes pronounced degradation in earlier tasks as the training progresses. Limiting ES to 100 iterations offers a balance. While it sacrifices a small degree of peak single task accuracy compared to the 300 iteration configuration, it maintains sequential training stability. Both ES (100) and GRPO remain comparatively stable throughout the entire sequential training pipeline, avoiding the sharp drop-offs seen with ES (300). Because of this, we use an iteration count of 100 for ES in all of the following sequential experiments.

As a side note, ES and GRPO show different transfer dynamics in the sequential task training. ES exhibits notable zero-shot forward transfer, i.e., learning a task increases performance on an unseen task. Chemistry accuracy rises from 63% to approximately 69% before its training stage begins, and Math accuracy increases by roughly 3 points after Countdown training alone. This forward transfer is not universal and depends on the tasks, as BoolQ accuracy dips slightly below the base model before its training stage. GRPO shows little forward transfer by comparison.

4.2 Forgetting

To test whether fine-tuning affects general capabilities beyond training tasks, we evaluate both methods on two held-out benchmarks after each training stage: MMLU for general knowledge, and IFEval (strict) for instruction-following ability. The two methods diverge on MMLU. ES accuracy drops monotonically from 77.5% to 73.8% across the four training stages (−-3.7%), with the largest single-stage drop during Chemistry training (−-1.6%). GRPO, by contrast, remains stable or slightly improves throughout, ending at 78.3% (++0.8%). On IFEval, the pattern reverses: ES gains ++2.2%, peaking after Math training, while GRPO rises through Chemistry but drops after BoolQ training, ending at −-1.3% below baseline.

We measure the incremental KL divergence KL(πafter∥πbefore)\text{KL}(\pi_{\text{after}}\|\pi_{\text{before}}) on each task’s held-out set after every training step, capturing how much each step shifts the model’s output distribution on every task (Figure 2). Qiu et al. (2025) find that ES produces substantially lower KL divergence than GRPO on a single-task conciseness benchmark. The first column of our heatmap (T0, Countdown only) is broadly consistent: ES’s on-task KL (0.23 nats) is slightly lower than GRPO’s (0.29 nats). In the sequential setting, however, ES produces larger off-diagonal KL shifts—training on any task causes non-trivial drift on all other tasks (e.g., training on Math shifts BoolQ by 0.23 nats for ES vs. 0.01 for GRPO). ES’s on-diagonal drift is also more aggressive: Chemistry training induces 1.10 nats for ES versus 0.07 for GRPO. GRPO’s drift remains localized, with all values below 0.29 nats and minimal off-diagonal interference. This is consistent with our weight-space findings: ES’s isotropic perturbations spread change broadly across the output distribution, while GRPO’s directed updates concentrate it on the trained task. The discrepancy with Qiu et al. (2025) in the sequential setting may reflect differences in task structure or model, but it suggests the KL advantage of ES is not universal.

5 Weight Space Geometry Analysis

Despite both ES and GRPO achieving similar accuracy when trained with a single task, their difference in the sequential task experiments suggests that the weight changes of both could be distinct. We characterize the geometry of their weight changes, seeking a deeper understanding of the difference between the two methods.

5.1 ES induces larger weight changes

We measure the total ℓ2\ell_{2} norm of each method’s weight delta from the base model:

‖Δ​θ‖2=‖θtrained−θbase‖2\|\Delta\theta\|_{2}=\|\theta_{\text{trained}}-\theta_{\text{base}}\|_{2} (2)

Table 3 shows this at each sequential checkpoint. ES updates grow from 87.28 to 173.00 across the four tasks, while GRPO updates remain two orders of magnitude smaller (1.00 to 1.84), yielding norm ratios of 87 to 107×\times.

5.2 ES and GRPO solutions are linearly connected

We evaluate whether ES and GRPO solutions occupy the same loss basin by testing linear interpolations (i.e. linear mode connectivity) at each sequential checkpoint:

θ⁡(α)=(1−α)​θES+α​θGRPO,α∈{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1}\theta(\alpha)=(1-\alpha)\,\theta_{\text{ES}}+\alpha\,\theta_{\text{GRPO}},\quad\alpha\in\{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1\} (3)

A loss barrier would manifest as degraded performance at intermediate α\alpha values relative to both endpoints. Figure 3 shows average accuracy across tasks at each interpolation point. No significant loss barrier exists at any checkpoint: performance transitions smoothly, and intermediate points frequently match or outperform both endpoints, demonstrating that ES and GRPO remain in the same loss basin throughout sequential training.

5.3 ES solution direction behaves similarly as random directions

To understand why ES and GRPO produce such different weight geometries despite similar task accuracy, we probe the loss landscape along each method’s learned update direction. Starting from the base model, we move along the normalized ES or GRPO weight delta at increasing magnitudes:

θperturbed=θbase+m⋅Δ​θ‖Δ​θ‖2\theta_{\text{perturbed}}=\theta_{\text{base}}+m\cdot\frac{\Delta\theta}{\|\Delta\theta\|_{2}} (4)

where mm ranges from 0 to ‖Δ​θ‖2\|\Delta\theta\|_{2} (the trained checkpoint) and beyond. Random directions, averaged over three seeds, serve as a control. By construction, m=‖Δ​θ‖2m=\|\Delta\theta\|_{2} exactly recovers the trained checkpoint.

Figure 4 shows that along the GRPO direction, task accuracy rises rapidly from the base-model level to the checkpoint level within a very small displacement, then degrades quickly once the perturbation magnitude exceeds the trained solution. Along the ES direction, accuracy improves more gradually over a much larger displacement scale, indicating that much of the ES displacement lies in directions only weakly coupled to the task. Both methods reach comparable final accuracy, but GRPO concentrates its useful signal into a much smaller norm, while ES spreads it across a larger perturbation that includes substantial task-irrelevant components.

Evaluating perturbed models on holdout tasks reinforces this picture (Figure 5). The ES direction and random directions produce similar holdout degradation profiles, confirming that the ES update is a diffuse shift rather than a targeted one. GRPO’s direction, though more effective on the target task, degrades general capabilities faster than either ES or random directions, consistent with its updates being concentrated in a narrow task-specific subspace.

6 Theoretical Interpretation

The preceding experiments reveal a consistent pattern: ES and GRPO reach comparable task accuracy, yet ES accumulates weight changes two orders of magnitude larger, its update direction resembles a random direction on holdout tasks, and the two solutions are linearly connected with no loss barrier. We now develop a theoretical account that explains all of these phenomena within a unified framework.

Central claim: signal–diffusion decomposition.

Idealizing ES as an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process under a quadratic potential with curvature QQ, the displacement after TT steps decomposes as (Prop. 4):

θES−θ0=(HT−I)​θ0⏟signal (GD-like)+∑t=1THt−1​ηT−t⏟diffusion,\theta_{\mathrm{ES}}-\theta_{0}=\underbrace{(H^{T}-I)\,\theta_{0}}_{\text{signal (GD-like)}}\;+\;\underbrace{\sum_{t=1}^{T}H^{t-1}\,\eta_{T-t}}_{\text{diffusion}}, (5)

with H:=I−α​σσR​QH:=I-\frac{\alpha\sigma}{\sigma_{R}}Q and i.i.d. noise ηt∼𝒩⁡(0,α2N​Id)\eta_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N}I_{d}). The first term drives parameters toward the optimum and resides in the column space of QQ, mirroring gradient descent; the second term is diffusion in dd dimensions. Along flat directions (𝐮\mathbf{u} where Q​𝐮=0Q\mathbf{u}=0), the signal vanishes while the diffusion persists. Noiseless gradient descent, by contrast, produces only the first term (Prop. 6).

Why diffusion dominates

On a flat landscape, the ES update is a pure random walk (Prop. 1): Δ​θt∼𝒩⁡(0,α2N​Id)\Delta\theta_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\,\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N}I_{d}), and

𝔼⁡[‖θT−θ0‖2]=α2​T​d/N.\mathbb{E}[\|\theta_{T}-\theta_{0}\|^{2}]={\alpha^{2}Td}/{N}. (6)

This scaling—linear in TT and dd, inverse in NN—persists in the off-manifold subspace even when the landscape has curvature. On linear and quadratic landscapes, we derive the full single-step statistics analytically (Prop. 2, 3). In linear case, the fraction of gradient-aligned squared displacement per step is (App. E.3):

ρ=(1+(N+1)​s)/(d+(N+1)​s),\rho={(1+(N{+}1)s)}\,/\,{(d+(N{+}1)s)}, (7)

where s:=σ2​‖𝐯‖2/σR2∈[0,1]s:=\sigma^{2}\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}/\sigma_{R}^{2}\in[0,1] is the signal fraction, with ‖𝐯‖\|\mathbf{v}\| the gradient norm. Since N≪dN\ll d in practice (N=30N=30, d≈4×109d\approx 4\times 10^{9}), ρ\rho is negligible. Over TT steps (Proposition 7):

𝔼​‖θES−θ0‖2=𝒪⁡(r)⏟on-manifold+α2​T​(d−r)/N⏟off-manifold≈α2​T​d/N.\mathbb{E}\|\theta_{\mathrm{ES}}-\theta_{0}\|^{2}=\underbrace{\mathcal{O}(r)}_{\text{on-manifold}}+\underbrace{{\alpha^{2}T(d{-}r)}/{N}}_{\text{off-manifold}}\approx{\alpha^{2}Td}/{N}. (8)

Geometric consequences

The decomposition yields a sharp hierarchy (Propositions 6–8):

‖θGD−θ0‖2=𝒪⁡(r),𝔼​‖θES−θ0‖2=𝒪⁡(r)+𝒪⁡(d),𝔼​‖θES−θGD‖2=𝒪⁡(d),\displaystyle\|\theta_{\mathrm{GD}}-\theta_{0}\|^{2}=\mathcal{O}(r),\qquad\mathbb{E}\|\theta_{\mathrm{ES}}-\theta_{0}\|^{2}=\mathcal{O}(r)+\mathcal{O}(d),\qquad\mathbb{E}\|\theta_{\mathrm{ES}}-\theta_{\mathrm{GD}}\|^{2}=\mathcal{O}(d), (9)

and the expected cosine similarity scales as 𝒪⁡(r/d)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{r/d}) (Remark 9): nearly orthogonal despite similar task performance. The key behavioral difference is on flat directions: GD freezes at initialization while ES diffuses with variance α2​t/N\alpha^{2}t/N (Propositions 4, 5).

6.1 Empirical validation and explanatory power

Random walk scaling.  For the full parameter vector, ‖Δ​θ‖2\|\Delta\theta\|^{2} grows linearly with step count (r=0.9999r=0.9999 for ES vs. r=0.875r=0.875 for GRPO; Figure 6A). Inverting the slope to infer the effective dimension yields deff/dtotal=96.4%d_{\mathrm{eff}}/d_{\mathrm{total}}=96.4\%—nearly all dimensions behave as flat. Per-parameter analysis confirms this: 145 large weight matrices follow the scaling almost exactly (deff/d=0.968±0.014d_{\mathrm{eff}}/d=0.968\pm 0.014, R2=0.9999R^{2}=0.9999), while normalization parameters deviate strongly (deff/d=1.73±0.88d_{\mathrm{eff}}/d=1.73\pm 0.88; Appendix C.1, Fig. 10). The 3.6%3.6\% deficit is interpretable as the task-relevant fraction where curvature constrains the walk.

Explaining each observation.  Eq. (5) explains: Large update norms (Table 3): ES is dominated by the 𝒪⁡(d)\mathcal{O}(d) off-manifold term while GRPO stays at 𝒪⁡(r)\mathcal{O}(r), producing the ∼100×{\sim}100\times ratio.  Flat mode connectivity (Fig. 3): after convergence, the θES\theta_{\mathrm{ES}}–θGD\theta_{\mathrm{GD}} line lies in the off-manifold subspace where loss is flat.  ES resembles random (Fig. 4): dominant fraction of ES update comes from off-manifold random walk, explaining their similarity and smaller directional curvature along ES updates; Holdout degradation (Fig. 5): the fine-tuning landscape sits atop a broad plateau of base-task performance; off-manifold perturbations beyond a certain radius degrade general capabilities regardless of task relevance, explaining the matched ES–random degradation profiles. This picture is summarized in Figure 6B.

Remark 1.

This behavior connects to a broader phenomenon: Antognini and Sohl-Dickstein (2018) showed that high-dimensional OU processes are dominated by their flattest dimensions. Similar random-walk-like dynamics has been observed in SGD-trained neural network weights, evolution of Influenza virus (H3N2) and ES-optimized visual stimuli (Moore et al., 2018; Wang and Ponce, 2022a; Wang and Ponce, 2022b), suggesting high degeneracy on flat subspaces is a generic feature of high-dimensional landscapes.

7 Discussion

Our results reveal that ES and GRPO find geometrically distinct solutions despite equivalent task performance: near-orthogonal update directions and orders-of-magnitude norm differences. The random walk interpretation from Section 6 provides a unifying explanation: on the high-dimensional subspace of task-irrelevant directions, ES accumulates isotropic noise whose squared norm grows linearly with steps, while the task-relevant component remains small but sufficient for learning. These geometric differences imply that task-matched solutions found by different optimizers need not be equivalent in parameter space or in how they alter the model more broadly. More generally, our results suggest that weight-space geometry is itself an important object of study in post-training, because similar downstream accuracy can mask substantial differences in the structure and scale of the underlying update.

In the study, LLM is used for coding the experiments, analyzing the results, assisting mathematical derivation, and polishing the writing.

Appendix B Experimental Configurations

All experiments use Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with full-parameter fine-tuning, seed 42, and a maximum of 1,024 generated tokens. Each task uses a fixed training set of 200 prompts.

B.2 Single-Task Training Curves

Figure 7 and Figure 8 show train and test reward over the course of single-task training for GRPO and ES using the configurations selected in Tables 4 and 5. Both methods converge on all four tasks without overfitting, confirming that these hyperparameters yield stable learning before we proceed to the sequential setting.

B.3 Selected Training Configurations

The selected configurations are summarized in Table 6. In the single-task setting, ES trains for 300 steps and GRPO for 20 epochs. In the sequential setting, each of the four tasks trains for 100 ES steps or 20 GRPO epochs with identical per-task hyperparameters.

All evaluations use greedy decoding (temperature =0=0) with a maximum of 1,024 generated tokens and binary rewards (1.0 correct, 0.0 otherwise). Table 7 summarizes the answer extraction and scoring for each task. Countdown problems are sourced from Jiayi-Pan/Countdown-Tasks-3to4, MATH from nlile/hendrycks-MATH-benchmark, SciKnowEval Chemistry from hicai-zju/SciKnowEval v2, BoolQ from google/boolq, MMLU from cais/mmlu, and IFEval from google/IFEval.

MMLU and IFEval are evaluated after training to measure whether general capabilities are preserved.

Appendix C Detailed Validation of Theoretical Predictions

C.1 Weight Drift in ES and GRPO Fine-tuning

Setup

We fine-tune a Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 language model (d=4,022,468,096d=4{,}022{,}468{,}096 parameters) on a single reasoning task using two optimizers:

  • •

    Evolution Strategy (ES): z-scored ES with perturbation standard deviation σ=0.0015\sigma=0.0015, step size α=σ/2=7.5×10−4\alpha=\sigma/2=7.5\times 10^{-4}, and population size N=30N=30. Training runs for T=500T=500 steps. Training run was extended from 300 steps to 500 steps for further evaluation here.

  • •

    GRPO: Group Relative Policy Optimization, a gradient-based RL fine-tuning method, run for T=20T=20 steps.

At each training step tt we record, for every named parameter θ(k)\theta^{(k)},

‖Δ​θt(k)‖2:=‖θt(k)−θ0(k)‖2,\|\Delta\theta^{(k)}_{t}\|^{2}:=\|\theta^{(k)}_{t}-\theta^{(k)}_{0}\|^{2},

the squared Euclidean distance from initialization.

Whole-model Drift vs. Theory (Figure 9)

Proposition 1 predicts that, on a flat landscape, the total squared drift grows linearly in step tt:

𝔼⁡[‖Δ​θt‖2]=α2​t​dN.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\Delta\theta_{t}\|^{2}\right]=\frac{\alpha^{2}\,t\,d}{N}.

Figure 9 plots the empirical ∑k‖Δ​θt(k)‖2\sum_{k}\|\Delta\theta^{(k)}_{t}\|^{2} against this theoretical curve. For ES the match is near-perfect:

R2=0.9943,r=0.9999,R^{2}=0.9943,\quad r=0.9999,

with an inferred theoretical slope of α2​d/N=75.42\alpha^{2}d/N=75.42 per step and an empirical slope of 72.7472.74, corresponding to an effective dimension ratio

deffd=0.964.\frac{d_{\mathrm{eff}}}{d}=0.964.

The 3.6%3.6\% deficit potentially reflects task relevant dimensions, where higher loss curvature constrained the random walk (Prop. 4), so the weight drift is smaller than random walk scaling.

GRPO exhibits drift four orders of magnitude smaller than ES (peak ‖Δ​θ‖2≈1.1\|\Delta\theta\|^{2}\approx 1.1 vs. ≈36,000\approx 36{,}000 for ES at step 500), confirming that gradient-based fine-tuning makes highly targeted updates rather than diffusing through parameter space.

Per-parameter Effective Dimension

To characterize which parameters drive the drift, we fit a no-intercept linear regression

‖Δ​θt(k)‖2≈s(k)⋅t\|\Delta\theta^{(k)}_{t}\|^{2}\approx s^{(k)}\cdot t

for each parameter kk independently, obtaining slope s(k)s^{(k)} and goodness of fit Rk2R^{2}_{k}. The effective random walk dimension of parameter kk is then defined by inverting Proposition 1:

deff(k):=s(k)​Nα2=4​s(k)​Nσ2,ρ(k):=deff(k)d(k),d^{(k)}_{\mathrm{eff}}:=\frac{s^{(k)}\,N}{\alpha^{2}}=\frac{4\,s^{(k)}\,N}{\sigma^{2}},\qquad\rho^{(k)}:=\frac{d^{(k)}_{\mathrm{eff}}}{d^{(k)}},

where d(k)d^{(k)} is the number of elements in parameter kk. A value ρ(k)≈1\rho^{(k)}\approx 1 indicates the parameter diffuses isotropically as predicted; ρ(k)≪1\rho^{(k)}\ll 1 indicates constrained random walk; ρ(k)>1\rho^{(k)}>1 indicates excess diffusion relative to dimension (potentially due to the effect of gradient-like drift, Prop. 3).

Large weight matrices.

Among the 145 large weight parameters (embedding, qkv_proj, o_proj, gate_up_proj, down_proj), the effective dimension ratio is

ρ=0.968±0.014(mean±std),R2=0.9999±0.0000.\rho=0.968\pm 0.014\quad(\text{mean}\pm\text{std}),\quad R^{2}=0.9999\pm 0.0000.

These parameters behave essentially as isotropic random walkers, confirming the flat-landscape assumption of Proposition 1.

Norm and layer-norm parameters.

The remaining 145 parameters (RMSNorm weights q_norm, k_norm, input_layernorm, post_attention_layernorm, norm) show highly variable behavior:

  • •

    q_norm / k_norm (128 elements each): ρ=2.46±0.33\rho=2.46\pm 0.33 and 2.00±0.502.00\pm 0.50 respectively, with R2≈0.8R^{2}\approx 0.8. The excess drift (ρ>1\rho>1) likely reflects a higher signal-to-noise ratio in these low-dimensional subspaces.

  • •

    input_layernorm / post_attention_layernorm: ρ≈0.97\rho\approx 0.97 and 1.551.55 on average, but with standard deviations ≳0.9\gtrsim 0.9 and strongly negative R2R^{2}, indicating non-linear, non-diffusive dynamics.

  • •

    model.norm: ρ=0.10\rho=0.10, R2=0.83R^{2}=0.83 — this single output norm is largely frozen by ES updates.

Appendix D Theoretical Results

D.1 Evolution Strategy on a Flat Landscape

Proposition 1 (Evolution Strategy on a Flat Landscape).

Let R⁡(θ)=constR(\theta)=\text{const}, so all reward variation arises from observation noise. Under the ES update Δ​θ=αN​∑i=1NZi​ϵi\Delta\theta=\frac{\alpha}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}\epsilon_{i} with ϵi∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)\epsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) and z-scored rewards ZiZ_{i}, the weight update is a pure isotropic random walk:

Δ​θ∼𝒩⁡(0,α2N​Id),𝔼⁡[‖Δ​θ‖2]=α2​dN.\Delta\theta\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\,\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N}I_{d}\right),\qquad\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\Delta\theta\|^{2}\bigr]=\frac{\alpha^{2}d}{N}.

After TT steps of ES with population size NN, step size α\alpha, and parameter dimension dd, the cumulative deviation satisfies

𝔼⁡[‖θT−θ0‖2]=α2​T​dN=σ2​T​d4​N,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\theta_{T}-\theta_{0}\|^{2}\bigr]=\frac{\alpha^{2}Td}{N}=\frac{\sigma^{2}Td}{4N},

where the last equality substitutes α=σ/2\alpha=\sigma/2. In particular, the expected drift grows linearly in TT and dd, and shrinks inversely in the batch size NN. Proof in E.2.

D.2 Evolution Strategy on a Linear Landscape

Proposition 2 (Evolution Strategy on a Linear Landscape).

Let R⁡(θ)=−𝐯⊤​θR(\theta)=-\mathbf{v}^{\top}\theta with observation noise σξ\sigma_{\xi}. Define σR2:=σ2​‖𝐯‖2+σξ2\sigma_{R}^{2}:=\sigma^{2}\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}+\sigma_{\xi}^{2}. The mean and covariance of the ES parameter update are

𝔼⁡[Δ​θ]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\Delta\theta] =−α​σ​𝐯σR\displaystyle=\frac{-\alpha\sigma\,\mathbf{v}}{\sigma_{R}} (10)
Cov⁡[Δ​θ]\displaystyle\operatorname{Cov}[\Delta\theta] =α2N​Id+α2​σ2N​σR2​𝐯𝐯⊤\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N}\,I_{d}+\frac{\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}}{N\sigma_{R}^{2}}\,\mathbf{v}\mathbf{v}^{\top} (11)

The mean update is purely aligned with the gradient direction 𝐯\mathbf{v}, and the covariance consists of the same isotropic baseline as the flat landscape plus a rank-1 boost along 𝐯\mathbf{v}. Relative to the quadratic case (Proposition 3), the linear landscape produces identical expressions with Q2=0Q^{2}=0: the curvature-dependent inflation of σR2\sigma_{R}^{2} and the anisotropic noise term 2​σ4​Q22\sigma^{4}Q^{2} are both absent. Proof in E.3.

Remark 2 (On-manifold alignment of ES update).

Define the signal fraction s:=σ2​‖𝐯‖2/σR2∈[0,1]s:=\sigma^{2}\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}/\sigma_{R}^{2}\in[0,1]. The on-manifold fraction of total squared displacement is

ρ:=𝔼​‖P∥​Δ​θ‖2𝔼​‖Δ​θ‖2=1+(N+1)​sd+(N+1)​s.\rho:=\frac{\mathbb{E}\|P^{\parallel}\Delta\theta\|^{2}}{\mathbb{E}\|\Delta\theta\|^{2}}=\frac{1+(N+1)\,s}{d+(N+1)\,s}.

Hence: (i) without signal (s=0s=0), ρ=1/d\rho=1/d, i.e. the update is purely diffusive; (ii) in the high-SNR limit (s→1s\to 1), ρ→(N+2)/(d+N+1)\rho\to(N+2)/(d+N+1); (iii) ρ\rho increases monotonically in ss and NN, and decreases in dd. Since N≪dN\ll d in practice, on-manifold movement per step is negligible relative to off-manifold diffusion.

D.3 Evolution Strategy on a Quadratic Landscape

Proposition 3 (Evolution Strategy on a Quadratic Landscape).

Let R⁡(θ)=−12​θ⊤​Q​θR(\theta)=-\frac{1}{2}\theta^{\top}Q\theta, current iterate θ0\theta_{0}, and 𝐯:=Q​θ0\mathbf{v}:=Q\theta_{0} (the negative gradient). Define

σR2:=σ2​‖𝐯‖2+σ42​Tr⁡[Q2]+σξ2.\sigma_{R}^{2}:=\sigma^{2}\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}+\tfrac{\sigma^{4}}{2}\operatorname{Tr}[Q^{2}]+\sigma_{\xi}^{2}. (12)

The mean and covariance of the ES parameter update are

𝔼⁡[Δ​θ]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\Delta\theta] =−α​σ​𝐯σR,\displaystyle=\frac{-\alpha\sigma\,\mathbf{v}}{\sigma_{R}}, (13)
Cov⁡[Δ​θ]\displaystyle\operatorname{Cov}[\Delta\theta] =α2N​σR2​(σ2​𝐯𝐯⊤+2​σ4​Q2+σR2​Id).\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N\sigma_{R}^{2}}\left(\sigma^{2}\,\mathbf{v}\mathbf{v}^{\top}+2\sigma^{4}Q^{2}+\sigma_{R}^{2}\,I_{d}\right). (14)

Relative to the linear case (Proposition 2), the quadratic term QQ introduces two additional contributions: (i) a curvature-dependent inflation of σR2\sigma_{R}^{2} through Tr⁡[Q2]\operatorname{Tr}[Q^{2}], which attenuates the mean gradient step; and (ii) an anisotropic noise term 2​σ4​Q2/σR22\sigma^{4}Q^{2}/\sigma_{R}^{2} in the covariance, which increases update variance along the principal high curvature directions of QQ. Proof in E.4.

Remark 3 (On-manifold alignment on quadratic landscape).

The on-manifold fraction of total expected squared displacement is

ρ=(N+1)​σ2​‖𝐯‖2+2​σ4​𝐯^⊤​Q2​𝐯^+σR2(N+1)​σ2​‖𝐯‖2+2​σ4​Tr⁡[Q2]+d​σR2,\rho=\frac{(N+1)\,\sigma^{2}\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}+2\sigma^{4}\,\hat{\mathbf{v}}^{\top}Q^{2}\hat{\mathbf{v}}+\sigma_{R}^{2}}{(N+1)\,\sigma^{2}\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}+2\sigma^{4}\,\operatorname{Tr}[Q^{2}]+d\,\sigma_{R}^{2}},

where 𝐯^:=𝐯/‖𝐯‖\hat{\mathbf{v}}:=\mathbf{v}/\|\mathbf{v}\|. Setting Q2=0Q^{2}=0 and σR2=σ2​‖𝐯‖2+σξ2\sigma_{R}^{2}=\sigma^{2}\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}+\sigma_{\xi}^{2} recovers the linear-landscape ratio ρ=(1+(N+1)​s)/(d+(N+1)​s)\rho=(1+(N{+}1)s)/(d+(N{+}1)s). The quadratic landscape modifies ρ\rho in two ways: the curvature inflates σR2\sigma_{R}^{2}, which grows the isotropic term d​σR2d\,\sigma_{R}^{2} in the denominator; and the 2​σ4​Q22\sigma^{4}Q^{2} noise splits between numerator (the projection 𝐯^⊤​Q2​𝐯^\hat{\mathbf{v}}^{\top}Q^{2}\hat{\mathbf{v}}) and denominator (the full trace Tr⁡[Q2]\operatorname{Tr}[Q^{2}]). When the gradient aligns with the high-curvature eigenvectors, much of the curvature-induced noise is on-manifold and ρ\rho is comparable to the linear case; when the curvature is predominantly orthogonal to 𝐯^\hat{\mathbf{v}}, the denominator grows while the numerator does not, suppressing ρ\rho.

D.4 Dynamics of ES on Quadratic Landscape

Proposition 4 (Dynamics of ES on Quadratic Landscape).

Consider the simplified evolution

θt+1=H​θt+ηt,ηt∼𝒩⁡(0,α2N​Id),\theta_{t+1}=H\theta_{t}+\eta_{t},\qquad\eta_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\tfrac{\alpha^{2}}{N}I_{d}\right),

where H=I−α​σσR​Q=∑k(1−α​σσR​λk)​𝐮k​𝐮k⊤H=I-\frac{\alpha\sigma}{\sigma_{R}}Q=\sum_{k}\left(1-\frac{\alpha\sigma}{\sigma_{R}}\lambda_{k}\right)\mathbf{u}_{k}\mathbf{u}_{k}^{\top}. 22 2 σR\sigma_{R} here is a fixed constant, not changing across iterations as in the full ES update (Eq. 12). Let γk:=1−α​σσR​λk\gamma_{k}:=1-\frac{\alpha\sigma}{\sigma_{R}}\lambda_{k} denote the contraction factor along eigendirection 𝐮k\mathbf{u}_{k}. Then the projected mean and variance evolve as

𝔼⁡[𝐮k⊤​θt]=γkt​𝐮k⊤​θ0,\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{u}_{k}^{\top}\theta_{t}]=\gamma_{k}^{t}\,\mathbf{u}_{k}^{\top}\theta_{0},
Var⁡[𝐮k⊤​θt]=α2N⋅{1−γk2​t1−γk2,γk2≠1,t,γk2=1.\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{u}_{k}^{\top}\theta_{t}]=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N}\cdot\begin{cases}\dfrac{1-\gamma_{k}^{2t}}{1-\gamma_{k}^{2}},&\gamma_{k}^{2}\neq 1,\\[6.0pt] t,&\gamma_{k}^{2}=1.\end{cases}

The process converges in mean and variance along direction 𝐮k\mathbf{u}_{k} if and only if |γk|<1|\gamma_{k}|<1, i.e.,

0<λk<2​σRα​σ.0<\lambda_{k}<\frac{2\sigma_{R}}{\alpha\sigma}.

In this regime, the asymptotic variance is

limt→∞Var⁡[𝐮k⊤​θt]=α2N⋅11−γk2,\lim_{t\to\infty}\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{u}_{k}^{\top}\theta_{t}]=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N}\cdot\frac{1}{1-\gamma_{k}^{2}},

and the convergence timescale is τk=−log2/logγk2\tau_{k}=-\log 2\,/\log\gamma_{k}^{2}. Proof in E.5.

Remark 4 (Stability conditions).

The three failure modes each correspond to a violation of |γk|<1|\gamma_{k}|<1. Flat directions (λk=0\lambda_{k}=0) satisfy γk=1\gamma_{k}=1, so both the mean and variance grow as a pure random walk: the optimizer drifts diffusively and never localizes. Concave directions (λk<0\lambda_{k}<0) give γk>1\gamma_{k}>1, causing exponential divergence of both mean and variance — the landscape actively repels the iterates. Overly sharp convex directions (λk≥2​σR/α​σ\lambda_{k}\geq 2\sigma_{R}/\alpha\sigma) give |γk|≥1|\gamma_{k}|\geq 1 for a different reason: the ES step overshoots, analogous to gradient descent with too large a learning rate. Note that because the ES learning rate is α=σ/2\alpha=\sigma/2, this threshold becomes λk=4​σR/σ2\lambda_{k}=4\sigma_{R}/\sigma^{2}.

Remark 5 (Optimal curvature).

Within the stable regime, the convergence speed and asymptotic variance are jointly controlled by γk2\gamma_{k}^{2}. Directions with λk≈σR/α​σ\lambda_{k}\approx\sigma_{R}/\alpha\sigma achieve γk≈0\gamma_{k}\approx 0, which simultaneously minimizes the convergence timescale (τk→1\tau_{k}\to 1 iteration) and the asymptotic variance (≈α2/N\approx\alpha^{2}/N). Directions near the stability boundary λk→0+\lambda_{k}\to 0^{+} or λk→(2​σR/α​σ)−\lambda_{k}\to(2\sigma_{R}/\alpha\sigma)^{-} suffer slow convergence and inflated variance. Thus the landscape curvature relative to the ratio σR/α​σ\sigma_{R}/\alpha\sigma plays the role of an effective condition number for the ES dynamics.

Remark 6 (Role of noise scale).

The asymptotic variance α2N⁡(1−γk2)\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N(1-\gamma_{k}^{2})} reveals the expected tension between exploration and precision: increasing the population size NN suppresses variance linearly, while the landscape geometry (through γk2\gamma_{k}^{2}) sets a floor on the minimum achievable uncertainty. In well-conditioned directions, 1−γk2≈2​α​σσR​λk1-\gamma_{k}^{2}\approx 2\frac{\alpha\sigma}{\sigma_{R}}\lambda_{k}, so the asymptotic variance scales as α​σR2​N​σ​λk\frac{\alpha\sigma_{R}}{2N\sigma\lambda_{k}}, inversely proportional to both curvature and the signal-to-noise ratio σ/σR\sigma/\sigma_{R}.

D.5 Dynamics of GD on Quadratic Landscape

Proposition 5 (Dynamics of GD on Quadratic Landscape).

Let R⁡(θ)=−12​θ⊤​Q​θR(\theta)=-\frac{1}{2}\theta^{\top}Q\theta with Q⪰0Q\succeq 0, and let gradient descent with learning rate β\beta iterate as θt+1=(I−β​Q)​θt\theta_{t+1}=(I-\beta Q)\,\theta_{t}. Define HGD:=I−β​QH_{\mathrm{GD}}:=I-\beta Q and let γkGD:=1−β​λk\gamma_{k}^{\mathrm{GD}}:=1-\beta\lambda_{k}. The iterate is

θt=HGDt​θ0=∑k=1d(γkGD)t​(𝐮k⊤​θ0)​𝐮k.\theta_{t}=H_{\mathrm{GD}}^{t}\,\theta_{0}=\sum_{k=1}^{d}(\gamma_{k}^{\mathrm{GD}})^{t}\,(\mathbf{u}_{k}^{\top}\theta_{0})\,\mathbf{u}_{k}.

Direction 𝐮k\mathbf{u}_{k} converges if and only if |γkGD|<1|\gamma_{k}^{\mathrm{GD}}|<1, i.e., 0<λk<2/β0<\lambda_{k}<2/\beta. In this regime the convergence timescale is τkGD=−log2/log(γkGD)2\tau_{k}^{\mathrm{GD}}=-\log 2\,/\,\log(\gamma_{k}^{\mathrm{GD}})^{2}, and the residual error is exactly zero: limt→∞𝐮k⊤​θt=0\lim_{t\to\infty}\mathbf{u}_{k}^{\top}\theta_{t}=0. Proof in E.6.

Remark 7 (Stability conditions for GD).

The three failure modes mirror those of the ES dynamics (Proposition 4): flat directions (λk=0\lambda_{k}=0) give γkGD=1\gamma_{k}^{\mathrm{GD}}=1, so the iterate is frozen at 𝐮k⊤​θ0\mathbf{u}_{k}^{\top}\theta_{0} for all tt — unlike ES, where the iterate drifts diffusively. Concave directions (λk<0\lambda_{k}<0) give γkGD>1\gamma_{k}^{\mathrm{GD}}>1, causing exponential divergence. Overly sharp convex directions (λk≥2/β\lambda_{k}\geq 2/\beta) give |γkGD|≥1|\gamma_{k}^{\mathrm{GD}}|\geq 1, and the iterate overshoots with growing or non-decaying oscillations.

D.6 GD displacement is low-dimensional

Proposition 6 (GD displacement is low-dimensional).

Starting from θ0\theta_{0} on a rank-rr quadratic landscape (r≪dr\ll d), the GD displacement

θGD−θ0=∑k:λk>0[(1−βλk)T−1](𝐮k⊤θ0)𝐮k\theta_{\mathrm{GD}}-\theta_{0}=\sum_{k:\,\lambda_{k}>0}\bigl[(1-\beta\lambda_{k})^{T}-1\bigr](\mathbf{u}_{k}^{\top}\theta_{0})\,\mathbf{u}_{k}

lies entirely within the rr-dimensional column space of QQ, with ‖θGD−θ0‖2=𝒪⁡(r)\|\theta_{\mathrm{GD}}-\theta_{0}\|^{2}=\mathcal{O}(r).

D.7 ES displacement decomposes into signal and diffusion

Proposition 7 (ES displacement decomposes into signal and diffusion).

The ES displacement from initialization decomposes as

θES−θ0=(HEST−I)​θ0⏟signal (on-manifold)+∑t=1THESt−1​ηT−t⏟noise (all directions).\theta_{\mathrm{ES}}-\theta_{0}=\underbrace{(H_{\mathrm{ES}}^{T}-I)\theta_{0}}_{\text{signal (on-manifold)}}+\underbrace{\sum_{t=1}^{T}H_{\mathrm{ES}}^{t-1}\,\eta_{T-t}}_{\text{noise (all directions)}}.

The signal term lies within the column space of QQ, identical in structure to the GD displacement with β↔α​σ/σR\beta\leftrightarrow\alpha\sigma/\sigma_{R}. The noise term has support in all dd dimensions. For r≪dr\ll d and large TT,

𝔼​‖θES−θ0‖2=𝒪⁡(r)⏟on-manifold+α2​T​(d−r)N⏟off-manifold diffusion≈α2​T​dN.\mathbb{E}\|\theta_{\mathrm{ES}}-\theta_{0}\|^{2}=\underbrace{\mathcal{O}(r)}_{\text{on-manifold}}+\underbrace{\frac{\alpha^{2}T(d-r)}{N}}_{\text{off-manifold diffusion}}\approx\frac{\alpha^{2}Td}{N}.

D.8 ES–GD difference is off-manifold

Proposition 8 (ES–GD difference is off-manifold).

When both methods have converged on the active directions ((γkES)T≈(γkGD)T≈0(\gamma_{k}^{\mathrm{ES}})^{T}\approx(\gamma_{k}^{\mathrm{GD}})^{T}\approx 0), the expected squared difference between the two solutions is dominated by off-manifold diffusion:

𝔼​‖θES−θGD‖2≈α2​T​(d−r)N=𝒪⁡(d).\mathbb{E}\|\theta_{\mathrm{ES}}-\theta_{\mathrm{GD}}\|^{2}\approx\frac{\alpha^{2}T(d-r)}{N}=\mathcal{O}(d).
Remark 8 (Geometric summary).

The three pairwise squared distances satisfy the hierarchy (for r≪dr\ll d, large TT):

‖θGD−θ0‖2\displaystyle\|\theta_{\mathrm{GD}}-\theta_{0}\|^{2} =𝒪⁡(r),\displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(r),
𝔼​‖θES−θ0‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\theta_{\mathrm{ES}}-\theta_{0}\|^{2} =𝒪⁡(r)+𝒪⁡(d),\displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(r)+\mathcal{O}(d),
𝔼​‖θES−θGD‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\theta_{\mathrm{ES}}-\theta_{\mathrm{GD}}\|^{2} =𝒪⁡(d).\displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(d).

The GD displacement is low-dimensional and task-aligned. The ES displacement superposes a comparable on-manifold component with a much larger isotropic off-manifold diffusion. The ES–GD difference is dominated by the off-manifold term alone, since both methods converge to the same optimum within the active subspace. This accounts for the empirical observation that ES achieves similar task performance to GD (shared on-manifold signal) while being far from it in parameter space (off-manifold diffusion).

Remark 9 (Cosine similarity between displacements).

Since θGD−θ0\theta_{\mathrm{GD}}-\theta_{0} lies within the column space of QQ and the ES noise is zero-mean, the expected inner product picks up only the on-manifold signal of ES. For large TT with both converged on active directions, the expected cosine similarity satisfies

𝔼⁡[cos⁡∠⁡(θES−θ0,θGD−θ0)]∼𝒪⁡(r/d),\mathbb{E}\left[\cos\angle(\theta_{\mathrm{ES}}-\theta_{0},\;\theta_{\mathrm{GD}}-\theta_{0})\right]\sim\mathcal{O}\!\left(\sqrt{r/d}\right),

which is small for r≪dr\ll d: the two displacement vectors are nearly orthogonal despite leading to similar task performance.

Appendix E Detailed derivations of theoretical results

E.1 Z-score ES Update Setup

We detail the ES update rule as implemented in LLM fine-tuning. The update at step tt is

θt+1=θt+α⋅1N∑i=1NZiϵi\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}+\alpha\cdot\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}\epsilon_{i} (15)

where each ϵi∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)\epsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) is an independent Gaussian perturbation, and Zi=Ri−μRσRZ_{i}=\frac{R_{i}-\mu_{R}}{\sigma_{R}} is the z-scored return for the ii-th sample. Here, RiR_{i} is the reward, with μR\mu_{R} and σR\sigma_{R} denoting the mean and standard deviation of the RiR_{i} across the population. With slight abuse of notation we let R⁡(θt+σ​ϵi)R(\theta_{t}+\sigma\epsilon_{i}) be the true or expected reward at the perturbed location, and RiR_{i} the observed reward with certain observation noise. The step size is set to α=σ/2\alpha=\sigma/2, and a population size of N=30N=30 is typical. Defining the update increment as

Δθ=α⋅1N∑i=1NZiϵi\Delta\theta=\alpha\cdot\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}\epsilon_{i} (16)

the algorithm iterates as θt+1=θt+Δ​θ\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}+\Delta\theta.

E.2 Flat Landscape Analysis

Proof of Proposition 1.

The key assumption is that ZiZ_{i} is independent of ϵi\epsilon_{i}, i.e., Zi⟂ϵiZ_{i}\perp\epsilon_{i}. Then, conditioned on a set of ZiZ_{i},

Var⁡[Δ​θ|Zi]=(α2N2​∑i=1NZi2)​Id\mathrm{Var}\left[\Delta\theta\,\middle|\,Z_{i}\right]=\left(\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}^{2}\right)I_{d} (17)

and the distribution is isotropic Gaussian:

Δ​θ|Zi∼𝒩⁡(0,(α2N2​∑i=1NZi2)​Id)\Delta\theta|Z_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\left(\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}^{2}\right)I_{d}\right) (18)

By definition,33 3 Note that this constraint depends on the implementation of the z-score Zi=Ri−μRσRZ_{i}=\frac{R_{i}-\mu_{R}}{\sigma_{R}}. In our code, we compute the standard deviation as σR2=1N​∑i=1N(Ri−μR)2\sigma_{R}^{2}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(R_{i}-\mu_{R})^{2}. In the unbiased variance estimator (denominator N−1N-1), the identity reads ∑i=1NZi2=N−1\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}^{2}=N-1.

∑i=1NZi2\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}^{2} =∑i=1N(Ri−μRσR)2\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\frac{R_{i}-\mu_{R}}{\sigma_{R}}\right)^{2}
=1σR2​∑i=1N(Ri−μR)2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sigma_{R}^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(R_{i}-\mu_{R})^{2}
=N(or N−1 with unbiased estimator)\displaystyle=N\quad\text{(or $N-1$ with unbiased estimator)} (19)

Therefore, in general the scaling is:

Var⁡[Δ​θ|Zi]\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}[\Delta\theta|Z_{i}] =α2N2​N​Id\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N^{2}}N\,I_{d}
=α2N​Id\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N}I_{d} (20)

Since this is independent of ZiZ_{i}, it follows after marginalizing:

Δ​θ∼𝒩⁡(0,α2N​Id)\Delta\theta\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N}I_{d}\right) (21)
Var⁡[Δ​θ]=α2N​Id\mathrm{Var}[\Delta\theta]=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N}I_{d} (22)

On a flat loss, Δ​θ\Delta\theta is independent between steps, so after TT steps, the combined weight change is

Δ​θ¯T=θT−θ0=∑t=1TΔ​θt\bar{\Delta\theta}_{T}=\theta_{T}-\theta_{0}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Delta\theta_{t} (23)

and the total variance is

Var⁡[Δ​θ¯T]=α2​TN​Id\mathrm{Var}[\bar{\Delta\theta}_{T}]=\frac{\alpha^{2}T}{N}I_{d} (24)

The expected squared norm of total deviation is

𝔼​‖Δ​θ¯T‖2=α2​T​dN\mathbb{E}\|\bar{\Delta\theta}_{T}\|^{2}=\frac{\alpha^{2}Td}{N} (25)

Finally, substituting α=σ2\alpha=\frac{\sigma}{2} gives

α2N=σ24​N\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N}=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{4N} (26)

and

𝔼​‖Δ​θ¯T‖2=σ2​T​d4​N\mathbb{E}\|\bar{\Delta\theta}_{T}\|^{2}=\frac{\sigma^{2}Td}{4N} (27)

E.3 Linear Landscape Analysis

Proof of Proposition 2.

Consider a linear landscape with i.i.d. observational noise ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,1)\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), assumed independent of ϵ\epsilon, i.e., ξ⟂ϵ\xi\perp\epsilon. The linear reward is

R⁡(θ)=−𝐯⊤​θR(\theta)=-\mathbf{v}^{\top}\theta (28)

and the observed reward for each sample is

Ri\displaystyle R_{i} =R⁡(θ0+σ​ϵi)+σξ​ξi\displaystyle=R(\theta_{0}+\sigma\epsilon_{i})+\sigma_{\xi}\xi_{i}
=−𝐯⊤​(θ0+σ​ϵi)+σξ​ξi\displaystyle=-\mathbf{v}^{\top}(\theta_{0}+\sigma\epsilon_{i})+\sigma_{\xi}\xi_{i}
≡−σ​𝐯⊤​ϵi+σξ​ξi\displaystyle\equiv-\sigma\,\mathbf{v}^{\top}\epsilon_{i}+\sigma_{\xi}\xi_{i} (29)

Decompose the exploration as

ϵi=ϵi⟂+ϵi∥\displaystyle\epsilon_{i}=\epsilon_{i}^{\perp}+\epsilon_{i}^{\parallel} (30)

where

P⟂\displaystyle P^{\perp} :=I−𝐯𝐯⊤‖𝐯‖2\displaystyle:=I-\frac{\mathbf{v}\mathbf{v}^{\top}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}} (31)
P∥\displaystyle P^{\parallel} :=𝐯𝐯⊤‖𝐯‖2\displaystyle:=\frac{\mathbf{v}\mathbf{v}^{\top}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}} (32)

so that ϵi⟂:=P⟂​ϵi\epsilon_{i}^{\perp}:=P^{\perp}\epsilon_{i}, ϵi∥:=P∥​ϵi\epsilon_{i}^{\parallel}:=P^{\parallel}\epsilon_{i}. Then ϵi⟂∼𝒩⁡(0,P⟂)\epsilon_{i}^{\perp}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P^{\perp}), ϵi∥∼𝒩⁡(0,P∥)\epsilon_{i}^{\parallel}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P^{\parallel}), and ϵi⟂⟂ϵi∥\epsilon_{i}^{\perp}\perp\epsilon_{i}^{\parallel}.

The reward is

Ri\displaystyle R_{i} =−σ​𝐯⊤​ϵi∥+σξ​ξi\displaystyle=-\sigma\mathbf{v}^{\top}\epsilon_{i}^{\parallel}+\sigma_{\xi}\xi_{i} (33)

and thus Ri⟂ϵi⟂R_{i}\perp\epsilon_{i}^{\perp}.

The update is:

Δθ=α⋅1N∑i=1NZiϵi\Delta\theta=\alpha\cdot\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}\epsilon_{i} (34)

and can be split as

Δ​θ=P⟂​Δ​θ+P∥​Δ​θ\Delta\theta=P^{\perp}\Delta\theta+P^{\parallel}\Delta\theta (35)

Off-manifold component

P⟂​Δ​θ\displaystyle P^{\perp}\Delta\theta =α⋅1N∑i=1NZiP⟂ϵi\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}P^{\perp}\epsilon_{i}
=α⋅1N∑i=1NZiϵi⟂\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}\epsilon_{i}^{\perp} (36)

Conditioned on the observed normalized reward ZiZ_{i}, P⟂​Δ​θP^{\perp}\Delta\theta is a weighted sum of Gaussian random vectors, thus Gaussian:

P⟂​Δ​θ|{Zi}i=1N∼𝒩⁡(0,α2N2​∑i=1NZi2​P⟂)P^{\perp}\Delta\theta\mid\{Z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}^{2}P^{\perp}\right) (37)

Since {Zi}i=1N\{Z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} are z-scored {Ri}i=1N\{R_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}, the sum satisfies the following identity.

P⟂​Δ​θ|{Zi}i=1N∼𝒩⁡(0,α2N​P⟂)P^{\perp}\Delta\theta\mid\{Z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N}P^{\perp}\right) (38)

Because of the following equations:

σR2\displaystyle\sigma_{R}^{2} =1N​∑i=1N(Ri−μR)2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(R_{i}-\mu_{R})^{2} (39)
Zi\displaystyle Z_{i} =Ri−μRσR\displaystyle=\frac{R_{i}-\mu_{R}}{\sigma_{R}} (40)

Thus, the conditional distribution is

P⟂​Δ​θ|{Zi}i=1N∼𝒩⁡(0,α2N2​N​P⟂)P^{\perp}\Delta\theta\,\big|\;\{Z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N^{2}}NP^{\perp}\right) (41)

Since the conditional distribution P⟂​Δ​θ|{Zi}i=1NP^{\perp}\Delta\theta\,\big|\;\{Z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} is independent of the observed reward, marginalizing over ZiZ_{i} we have

P⟂​Δ​θ∼𝒩⁡(0,α2N​P⟂)P^{\perp}\Delta\theta\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N}P^{\perp}\right) (42)

The norm of the off-manifold component is

𝔼​‖P⟂​Δ​θ‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|P^{\perp}\Delta\theta\|^{2} =Tr⁡[α2N​P⟂]\displaystyle=\mathrm{Tr}\left[\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N}P^{\perp}\right]
=α2N​(d−1)\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N}(d-1) (43)

On-manifold component

P∥​Δ​θ\displaystyle P^{\parallel}\Delta\theta =α⋅1N∑i=1NZiP∥ϵi\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}P^{\parallel}\epsilon_{i}
=α⋅1N∑i=1NZiϵi∥\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}\epsilon_{i}^{\parallel} (44)

The on-manifold variable can be expressed as ϵi∥=𝐯‖𝐯‖​ni\epsilon_{i}^{\parallel}=\frac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|}n_{i}, with ni∼𝒩⁡(0,1)n_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), thus the reward can be written as

Ri\displaystyle R_{i} =−σ​𝐯⊤​ϵi∥+σξ​ξi\displaystyle=-\sigma\mathbf{v}^{\top}\epsilon_{i}^{\parallel}+\sigma_{\xi}\xi_{i}
=−σ​𝐯⊤​𝐯‖𝐯‖​ni+σξ​ξi\displaystyle=-\sigma\frac{\mathbf{v}^{\top}\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|}n_{i}+\sigma_{\xi}\xi_{i}
=−σ​‖𝐯‖​ni+σξ​ξi\displaystyle=-\sigma\|\mathbf{v}\|n_{i}+\sigma_{\xi}\xi_{i} (45)

Recall the definition of observed reward and z-score,

Zi=Ri−μRσRZ_{i}=\frac{R_{i}-\mu_{R}}{\sigma_{R}} (46)

To simplify derivation, we use the population expectation and standard deviation here:

μR\displaystyle\mu_{R} ≈𝔼⁡[Ri]=0\displaystyle\approx\mathbb{E}[R_{i}]=0 (47)
σR2\displaystyle\sigma_{R}^{2} ≈Var⁡[Ri]=σ2​‖𝐯‖2+σξ2\displaystyle\approx\mathrm{Var}[R_{i}]=\sigma^{2}\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}+\sigma_{\xi}^{2} (48)

Under these simplifications,

P∥​Δ​θ\displaystyle P^{\parallel}\Delta\theta =αN​∑i=1NZi​ϵi∥\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}\epsilon_{i}^{\parallel}
=αN​∑i=1N−σ​‖𝐯‖​ni+σξ​ξi−μRσR​ni​𝐯‖𝐯‖\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{-\sigma\|\mathbf{v}\|n_{i}+\sigma_{\xi}\xi_{i}-\mu_{R}}{\sigma_{R}}n_{i}\frac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|}

The expectation reads

𝔼⁡[P∥​Δ​θ]=\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[P^{\parallel}\Delta\theta]= αN​σR​∑i=1N𝔼⁡[(−σ​‖𝐯‖​ni+σξ​ξi)​ni]​𝐯‖𝐯‖\displaystyle~\frac{\alpha}{N\sigma_{R}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}\left[(-\sigma\|\mathbf{v}\|n_{i}+\sigma_{\xi}\xi_{i})n_{i}\right]\frac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|}
=\displaystyle= αN​σR𝔼[−σ∥𝐯∥∑i=1Nni2+σξ∑i=1Nξini]𝐯‖𝐯‖\displaystyle~\frac{\alpha}{N\sigma_{R}}\mathbb{E}[-\sigma\|\mathbf{v}\|\sum_{i=1}^{N}n_{i}^{2}+\sigma_{\xi}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\xi_{i}n_{i}]\frac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|}
=\displaystyle= αN​σR​(−σ​‖𝐯‖​N)​𝐯‖𝐯‖\displaystyle~\frac{\alpha}{N\sigma_{R}}(-\sigma\|\mathbf{v}\|N)\frac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|}

where we used independence, 𝔼⁡[ξi​ni]=0\mathbb{E}[\xi_{i}n_{i}]=0, and 𝔼⁡[∑i=1Nni2]=N\mathbb{E}[\sum_{i=1}^{N}n_{i}^{2}]=N.
